# Containers From First Principles: Namespaces, cgroups and Images

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against man7.org namespaces(7), unshare(1) and nsenter(1), the kernel cgroup v2 admin guide, the OCI image and runtime specs, the Bash manual, Docker and Kubernetes docs, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit and CUDA Compatibility docs. The `unshare` and `nsenter` commands were not run (macOS).

Scope: general container concepts (Linux, OCI, Docker-style tooling; OCI is the Open Container Initiative, the standards body that defines image and runtime formats).

Builds on: processes, the kernel and signals (module os-fundamentals). This lesson says nothing about how any particular company builds or runs its containers. In week 1, replace the generic nouns below with the real ones.

## The problem and why it matters

"It works on my machine" is a packaging problem: the code ran against one set of libraries, paths and settings, and production has another. A container packages a program together with the files it needs, and runs it with a restricted view of the machine.

The word "container" misleads people into picturing a small VM. It is not one. If you hold the wrong picture, you will mis-debug the three things that matter in production: why a process was killed at a memory limit, why a GPU workload fails on one host and not another, and why "the same image" behaved differently on Tuesday.

## First principles

1. **A container is a process.** On the host it shows up in `ps` like any other. There is no guest operating system and no hypervisor (the software that runs whole virtual machines). One kernel (the core of the OS, which owns memory, CPU and devices) runs everything. The host is the machine the containers run on.
2. **Namespaces limit what the process can see.** A namespace gives a process its own private view of one kind of resource: process IDs (PIDs), network devices, mount points (where filesystems attach to the directory tree), hostname, users, IPC objects (shared memory and message queues between processes), cgroup root, clocks. The kernel's namespace types are mount, UTS, IPC, PID, network, user, cgroup and time.
3. **cgroups limit what the process can use.** A control group (cgroup) puts processes under accounting and limits for memory, CPU, process count and more. Namespaces are about visibility; cgroups are about consumption. Different mechanisms.
4. **The root filesystem comes from an image.** The process sees a directory tree assembled from stacked, read-only layers plus a thin writable layer. Throw the container away and the writable layer goes too.
5. **Everything is content-addressed.** Layers, configs and manifests are identified by a hash of their bytes (a digest). A hash is a fixed-size fingerprint computed from data. A digest names exactly one thing. A tag is a movable label.
6. **Not isolated: the kernel.** Every container on a host shares its kernel, its drivers and its clock source. A kernel bug, a missing kernel feature or a mismatched GPU driver is shared by all of them.

## How it works

### One process, four wrappers

```
 ONE host kernel, shared by every container
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  process (host PID 4242, "PID 1" inside) │
 │                                          │
 │  namespaces  what it can SEE             │
 │   pid net mnt uts ipc user cgroup time   │
 │                                          │
 │  cgroup      what it can USE             │
 │   memory.max  cpu.max  pids.max          │
 │                                          │
 │  rootfs      what files it has           │
 │   image layers (ro) + writable layer     │
 │                                          │
 │  security    what it may DO              │
 │   capabilities, seccomp, user id         │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
 on macOS/Windows a hidden Linux VM supplies the
 kernel; the containers still share THAT kernel
```

You can build a toy container by hand. The commands below create fresh PID, mount, UTS and network namespaces. They were **not run** (this machine is macOS; they need Linux and root):

```bash
# Linux only. Not run here.
sudo unshare --fork --pid --mount-proc --uts --net sh
hostname demo      # changes only inside the new UTS namespace
echo $$            # prints 1: we are PID 1 in a new PID namespace
ps aux             # sees only this namespace's processes
ip link            # only a loopback device, no host NICs
```

`--fork` makes the program a child of `unshare`, which a new PID namespace needs. `--mount-proc` remounts `/proc` so `ps` reports the new namespace. To enter a running container's namespaces from the host, find its host PID and use `nsenter` (also not run):

```bash
sudo nsenter --target 4242 --net --pid --mount   # PID 4242 is a placeholder
ls -l /proc/4242/ns/                             # one handle per namespace
```

That is why `nsenter --net` is a common way to debug a container's networking with host tools.

### Images are layered, content-addressed filesystems

```
 image index (optional): one entry per platform
   └─▶ manifest  sha256:aaa…
        ├─ config   sha256:bbb…  env, cmd, user
        ├─ layer 1  sha256:c11…  base OS files
        ├─ layer 2  sha256:c22…  language runtime
        ├─ layer 3  sha256:c33…  dependencies
        └─ layer 4  sha256:c44…  your binary

 at run time:
   ┌────────────────────────┐
   │ writable layer (temp)  │ lost on removal
   ├────────────────────────┤
   │ layer 4   read-only    │
   │ layer 3   read-only    │ shared by all
   │ layer 2   read-only    │ containers using
   │ layer 1   read-only    │ the same layers
   └────────────────────────┘
```

In OCI terms, an image is a manifest (the document naming the config and layers by digest), a config (environment, entrypoint, layer order), a set of layers (each a changeset applied on top of the previous), and optionally an index (a list of manifests, usually one per CPU architecture). The OCI *runtime* spec is the second half: given a bundle (a root filesystem plus a `config.json`), a runtime such as `runc` creates the namespaces and cgroups and starts the process.

Two consequences. Layers are shared, so ten containers from one image do not store ten copies of the base. And a layer is immutable: deleting a file in a later layer hides it but does not shrink the image, because the earlier layer still holds the bytes.

### Registries, tags and digests

A registry (a server that stores and serves images) stores blobs and manifests under a name. `service:1.4` is a **tag**: a pointer that whoever has push rights can move. `service@sha256:…` is a **digest**: the hash of the manifest, so it can never mean anything else. Deployments you need to reproduce or audit should record the digest. A tag tells you what someone *intended*; a digest tells you what *ran*.

### What happens at a resource limit

```
 allocation request
        │
        ▼
 usage + new > memory.max ?
    │ no ─▶ granted
    │ yes
    ▼
 kernel tries to reclaim (page cache, swap if allowed)
    │ freed enough ─▶ granted, but slow
    │ cannot
    ▼
 OOM killer runs INSIDE the cgroup
    └─▶ victim gets SIGKILL (no handler runs)

 CPU limit: no kill. cpu.max = "quota period".
 Over quota in a period ─▶ threads sleep until the
 next period (throttling).
```

Here the page cache is memory the kernel uses to keep recently read file data, and swap is disk used as overflow memory. The OOM (out-of-memory) killer is the kernel routine that picks a process to kill. SIGKILL is the signal that ends a process immediately and cannot be caught.

Memory is a hard wall: reclaim fails and a process is killed. CPU is a rate: the process is paused, never killed, and shows up as latency. `memory.high` is a softer setting that throttles instead of killing. Docker's `--memory` and `--cpus` flags, and Kubernetes limits, set these cgroup files for you.

### The GPU case

The GPU driver lives in the host kernel (plus user-space libraries). A container image can ship the CUDA (NVIDIA's GPU programming platform) *toolkit and libraries*, but it cannot ship the kernel driver. The NVIDIA driver is installed on the host (the Container Toolkit install guide lists it as a prerequisite), and a tool such as the NVIDIA Container Toolkit injects the chosen GPU devices and other host-side mounts into the container when it starts. So the image's CUDA version needs a host driver that is new enough for it (NVIDIA's CUDA Compatibility docs call this "a sufficiently new driver"; the exact minimum depends on the versions involved, so look it up for yours). "Works on host A, fails on host B" is very often a driver mismatch.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** a service container restarts every few hours. The orchestrator (the system that starts, restarts and places containers, such as Kubernetes) says it exited with code 137. The logs just stop, with no error and no stack trace.

1. **Read 137 correctly.** Exit codes above 128 mean "killed by signal (code minus 128)". 137 is 128 + 9, SIGKILL. SIGKILL cannot be caught, so no log line is written. Something killed it; you do not yet know what.
2. **Who sends SIGKILL?** Candidates: the cgroup OOM killer, the host OOM killer, an operator, or the runtime (the program that starts and stops containers) after a stop timeout. Ask the platform for the termination *reason* (in Kubernetes, `OOMKilled` appears in the container's last state).
3. **Confirm in the kernel.** On the host, the container's cgroup `memory.events` file counts `oom_kill`. The kernel log (`dmesg`) names the victim. Both Linux-specific; not run here.
4. **Find the shape of growth.** A steady climb is a leak or an unbounded cache or queue. A sudden jump is a large input (a big payload decoded fully into memory). Compare the memory limit with what the process actually peaks at.
5. **Check what the limit really covers.** The cgroup counts page cache and kernel memory attributable to the group, not just your heap. A service that reads big files can approach the limit without a heap leak.
6. **Decide.** Fix the unbounded growth, bound the queue, stream instead of buffering, or raise the limit with a measured justification.

**Fix:** do not "just raise the limit" until step 4 tells you which shape you have. A limit raised against a leak only lengthens the time between restarts.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| You want the same runtime environment on a laptop, in CI and in production | You need a different kernel or kernel modules per workload (use a VM) |
| You run many small services and want fast start and dense packing | You run hostile, untrusted code (a shared kernel is a large attack surface) |
| You want immutable, versioned, rollback-able artifacts | The "container" would carry mutable state that must survive restarts, with no volume |
| You want per-workload resource limits on a shared host | A workload is so latency-sensitive that CPU throttling surprises you; reserve CPUs instead |

## Interview questions

1. What is a container, technically? *Probe:* how is it different from a VM? *Outline:* a process with namespaces (visibility), cgroups (usage), a layered root filesystem and a restricted security context (Linux capabilities, which split root's powers into small pieces, and seccomp, a filter on which system calls are allowed); one shared kernel.
2. What is the difference between a namespace and a cgroup? *Outline:* what a process can see versus what it can consume; name a few namespace types and a few cgroup controllers.
3. What happens when a container hits its memory limit versus its CPU limit? *Probe:* which one produces a restart and which one produces latency? *Outline:* memory: reclaim fails, OOM killer, SIGKILL. CPU: throttling by quota per period.
4. Why use a digest instead of a tag in production? *Outline:* tags are mutable pointers; a digest is the content hash; reproducibility and audit.
5. A GPU container works on one node and fails on another. What do you check? *Outline:* driver version on the host versus the CUDA version in the image, device files exposed, container toolkit configured, the same image digest on both.
6. Why does deleting a file in a later Dockerfile instruction not shrink the image? *Outline:* layers are immutable changesets; the earlier layer still holds the data.

**Worked exercise:** on paper, list the eight namespace types and say, for each, one thing a container loses sight of. Then explain how you would prove, using only `/proc` and cgroup files on a Linux host, that a given container was OOM-killed.

## Checklist

1. I can say a container is a process plus namespaces, cgroups and a layered rootfs.
2. I can name what is not isolated (the kernel) and why that matters for GPUs.
3. I can explain layers, manifests, tags and digests in one minute.
4. I can predict what happens at a memory limit and at a CPU limit.
5. I can read exit code 137 and name the next three checks.

## Common wrong answers

- "A container is a lightweight VM." It has no guest kernel.
- "Containers are isolated, so a kernel bug can't cross them." The kernel is shared.
- "`latest` is the newest build." It is just a tag and means whatever was last pushed under it.
- "Raise the limit and the OOM goes away." Only if the growth is bounded.
- "CPU limits kill the process like memory limits." They throttle it.

## Sources

Consulted and checked:

- man7.org `namespaces(7)`: the eight namespace types and their clone flags; `/proc/[pid]/ns` and `setns`.
- man7.org `unshare(1)` and `nsenter(1)`: the flags used above (`--fork`, `--pid`, `--mount-proc` which implies a mount namespace, `--uts`, `--net`, `--target`).
- kernel.org cgroup v2 admin guide: `memory.max` (OOM killer invoked in the cgroup when usage cannot be reduced), `memory.high` (throttles, never invokes the OOM killer), `memory.events` (`oom_kill`), `cpu.max`, `pids.max`; `memory.current` includes page cache and kernel data structures.
- OCI image spec (image index, platform with architecture and os) and runtime spec (bundle = `config.json` plus root filesystem).
- Docker docs, resource constraints: `--memory`, `--cpus`, kernel kills processes on OOM by default. Docker Desktop docs: containers run in a Linux VM.
- Bash manual, Exit Status: a command killed by a fatal signal N gives exit status 128+N, so 137 is SIGKILL (9).
- Kubernetes memory-limit task page: `OOMKilled` in `lastState.terminated.reason` with `exitCode: 137`; the kubelet restarts the container.
- NVIDIA Container Toolkit install guide (host driver is a prerequisite), architecture overview (injects devices and mounts), CUDA Compatibility docs ("sufficiently new driver").

Not run: the `unshare` and `nsenter` commands (macOS; they need Linux and root). Their flags were checked against the man pages. Not found in NVIDIA's docs: a statement of exactly which driver libraries are mounted into containers; the lesson no longer claims it.
